title: Southern Taurids Meteor Shower Begins: How to Catch a Fireball
summary:
One of the longest-running meteor showers of the year is officially underway. The Southern Taurids began on Sunday (Sept. 20) and will send occasional shooting stars — and potentially spectacular fireballs — across the night sky until Nov. 20.

This shower isn't about volume. During its peak, you can expect only about five to 10 meteors per hour, according to the American Meteor Society. But the Taurids have a reputation for producing fireballs — very bright meteors that flash as they fall through the atmosphere. Patience is often rewarded with some of the most impressive meteors of the year. That's partly because Southern Taurid meteors strike Earth's atmosphere at a relatively leisurely pace of around 17 miles per second (27 kilometers per second). That means they stay visible longer than most meteors and can leave glowing trails behind them.

The Southern Taurids are associated with a trail of rocky debris left in the inner solar system by Comet 2P/Encke, according to NASA. Their companion shower, the Northern Taurids, becomes active later in the fall, creating an extended period when Earth encounters debris from the same complex.

The shower peaks overnight on both Oct. 13-14 and Nov. 4-5. Sky conditions will be ideal: Oct. 13-14 will have a moonless night sky, and on Nov. 5 an 18%-lit waning crescent moon rises in the early morning. You'll still need a clear night, though. The rates will be too low for most city dwellers to justify a trip to a dark location.

Southern Taurid meteors appear to radiate from the constellation Taurus, which climbs higher as the night progresses. But there's no need to stare directly at it. Meteors can appear anywhere overhead, so a wide, unobstructed view of the sky is more useful. Stargazing binoculars and telescopes won't help you spot meteors — though they may come in handy for other fall skywatching treats. Because the shower's radiant lies close to the ecliptic, the Southern Taurids are observable from both hemispheres, but Northern Hemisphere observers generally enjoy better viewing conditions. Don't expect celestial fireworks; the Southern Taurids are a slow burn. But with brilliant fireballs possible, they're worth keeping an eye on whenever you're outside after dark this fall.
why_it_matters: Meteor showers are one of the few scientific events anyone can observe without equipment, which makes them a gateway into astronomy — and studying debris streams like the Taurids helps scientists understand the comets that cross Earth's orbit, both as harmless light shows and as objects worth tracking carefully.

background_read: Meteor showers happen when Earth crosses the dusty trail of debris a comet leaves behind in its orbit; the grit burns up in the atmosphere and looks like a shooting star, and an unusually bright one is called a fireball.
The American Meteor Society is a nonprofit group of amateur and professional skywatchers that collects meteor reports from the public and publishes yearly shower forecasts.

The Taurids come from Comet 2P/Encke, named after the astronomer Johann Franz Encke, who worked out its orbit in the 1800s. It circles the Sun faster than almost any other known comet, which is why its debris is spread so widely along Earth's path.

Taurus is one of the oldest star patterns people have recognized — a zodiac constellation shaped like a bull — and because it sits near the ecliptic, the line the Sun and planets trace across the sky, this shower can be seen from both hemispheres.
Skywatchers have recorded the Taurids for well over a century, and the shower is known less for its numbers than for the occasional brilliant fireballs it produces.

perspectives.description: For beginners the shower is ideal: no telescope, no cost and a chance at a spectacular fireball. Because the Taurids can be seen from both hemispheres across two months, almost anyone on Earth can take part.

Five to 10 meteors an hour means long stretches of nothing, and light pollution in cities can hide even the brightest ones. The fireball reputation may also oversell what most people will actually see on a given night.

The Taurids are a long-studied debris stream tied to a comet whose orbit is unusually short, and they have been reported for generations. That makes them useful for tracking how comets shed material and how Earth's orbit intersects those trails year after year.

Researchers continue to watch for years when the Taurid stream produces stronger fireball activity, and public reports to groups like the American Meteor Society help map that debris. The same monitoring techniques are used to study the small fraction of space rocks that could pose a real risk.
